draft:
The live technology-policy question is no longer whether manufacturers will retain technical control over products after sale. Many already design devices whose useful functions depend on continuing permission (features authenticated by software, accounts, or remote services). The harder question is whether the law should treat that arrangement as full ownership. It should not. When a maker can reach back through the network and disable part of what was sold, the buyer holds something less than the whole product—a deed with a trapdoor under it.

Remote control can serve legitimate purposes. A company may need to repair a dangerous flaw, protect compromised credentials, or stop abuse (especially when one defective component threatens other systems). But a useful maintenance channel does not settle who has final authority. The same connection that delivers a patch can withdraw a capability. If the maker keeps that power after accepting the purchase price, it’s retained control, however polished the purchase screen may look.

The distinction matters because ownership allocates risk. A buyer pays once, plans around the device, and bears the cost when it fails. The manufacturer, meanwhile, may preserve the ability to change the bargain (through a server setting rather than a physical recall). That arrangement doesn’t merely add a service layer. It lets one party rewrite the practical boundaries of property after the transaction—without returning the money or obtaining fresh consent.

Consider the ordinary pressure test. If a feature disappears tomorrow, who gets to decide whether the device still performs the job for which it was bought? The answer can’t depend entirely on the seller’s current business model (or on whether the relevant account still exists). A product that works only while its maker permits it to work resembles a rented room: the occupant may possess the key, but someone else still controls the lock.

Supporters of remote administration can reasonably point to security, fraud prevention, and legal compliance. Those concerns are real, yet they do not justify an unlimited power to erase purchased functionality. A narrowly tailored response to a concrete threat is different from a standing entitlement to reduce a product’s capabilities (including capabilities advertised at sale). Security should not become a label pasted over every post-sale restriction. Precision matters because the mechanism itself is powerful.

This is also why disclosure alone won’t solve the problem. A dense notice saying that features may change doesn’t create meaningful bargaining power, particularly when the device has already been installed or integrated with other equipment (and replacement carries its own cost). Nor should consent be inferred from a required click. You may technically accept the condition, but acceptance under those circumstances does not transform revocable access into durable ownership.

Policy should separate necessary intervention from commercial convenience. Makers may need authority to address a specific vulnerability (with notice, limits, and a path to restoration), but they shouldn’t be free to disable lawful, purchased functions merely because continued support has become inconvenient. Regulators can enforce representations made at sale, require refunds when essential capabilities are withdrawn, and protect independent repair (including access needed to keep abandoned products working).

We should adopt the narrower rule: if a seller wants continuing power to revoke a feature, it must describe the transaction as conditional access and price it accordingly. Our law cannot call the device fully sold while leaving its essential switches in the maker’s hands. A completed sale should transfer meaningful control of the product—not just possession until a distant server says otherwise.
